summary: This is easy: you register the app yourself with no provider review or payment, so your own account can connect within minutes. The main thing that can hold up launch is organization approval, because members of an organization with OAuth app restrictions cannot connect until an owner approves your app.
timeToTest: ~15 minutes, once your account's email is verified
timeToProduction: Immediately for personal-account users and organizations without restrictions.

gates.title: Any GitHub account can register the app
No test mode; the app works as soon as it is registered
No GitHub review before users can connect
Organizations with OAuth app restrictions must approve your app
gates.what: Members and outside collaborators of an organization with restrictions cannot authorize your app for that organization's resources. Unapproved apps get no API access to private organization resources.
gates.where: Organization settings, OAuth app policy. An org owner approves or denies each request.
gates.todo: Tell users in restricted orgs to request approval from an owner, and prepare that request text.

gates.title: No paid plan needed for production

requirements.text: A GitHub account with a verified email address, since users must verify email before they can authorize an OAuth app
A GitHub personal account or an organization where you have admin access to register the app under
A public homepage URL and one or more callback URLs your app serves

steps.text: Open Settings, then Developer settings, then OAuth apps, then New OAuth App
steps.why: Registering under a personal account or an org you administer is the only route the docs describe.
steps.detail: Owners can register up to 100 apps per user or organization.

steps.text: Enter the Application name and Homepage URL
steps.why: Users see these on the authorization page, so the docs say to use only public information.
steps.detail: Do not put internal URLs in any field.

steps.text: Enter the Authorization callback URL, adding more with Add callback URL if needed
steps.why: The callback URL is where GitHub sends users after they authorize. Redirect mismatches fail, so the URL must match what your code sends.
steps.detail: Up to 10 callback URLs are allowed.

steps.text: Leave Expire user access tokens enabled unless your code cannot handle expiring tokens yet
steps.why: Short-lived tokens with refresh are the safer default. The docs say OAuth app tokens are long-lived by default, and expiring tokens are an option you choose.
steps.detail: Turning it off makes tokens last indefinitely.

steps.text: Click Register application and save the client ID and client secret
steps.why: The secret must stay on your server.
steps.detail: Never put the client secret in client-side or user-device code.

steps.text: Verify your own account can authorize the app end to end
steps.why: This confirms the callback and scopes work before any user connects.
steps.detail: Your account must have a verified email address first.

steps.text: Draft the text users in restricted orgs send to request owner approval
steps.why: Owners approve from their OAuth app policy page, so users need to know what to ask for.

steps.text: Wait for an org owner to approve your app, if you need that org's data
steps.why: Only the org owner controls this.
steps.detail: Users in unrestricted orgs are not affected.

blockers.problem: Users cannot authorize because their email is unverified
blockers.fix: Ask them to verify their email address on GitHub, then retry.

blockers.problem: Authorization fails with a flagged-account message
blockers.fix: The message comes from an account restriction, not from email, org approval, or SAML. Retrying will not help. The user must follow GitHub's appeal process.

blockers.problem: Your app hits the token request cap and users get errors
blockers.fix: Cache tokens and avoid re-signing users. The cap is 2,000 token requests per hour for OAuth apps.
GitHub suspended the app for reported abuse, spam, or API misuse. Contact GitHub support through the link in the error, as the docs describe.

couldNotVerify: Whether the Enterprise Server 3.0 suspension wording matches github.com today
